cymbospondylus:enwiki:5.title: Cymbospondylus (Specimens that may belong to the genus)

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus lived during the Olenekian to Anisian stages of the Triassic period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Olenekian-Anisian~

facts.statement: The genus Cymbospondylus was named and described by Joseph Leidy in 1868.
facts.quote: authority: Leidy, 1868

facts.statement: The first fossils of Cymbospondylus were discovered in the 19th century in Nevada, United States.
facts.quote: The first known fossils of this taxon are a set of more or less complete vertebrae which were discovered in the 19th century in various mountain ranges of Nevada, in the United States, before being named and described by Joseph Leidy in 1868.

facts.statement: More complete fossils of Cymbospondylus were discovered in the early 20th century by the University of California and described by John Campbell Merriam in 1908.
facts.quote: It is in the beginning of the 20th century that more complete fossils were discovered through several expeditions to the Fossil Hill Member launched by the University of California, and described in more detail by John Campbell Merriam in 1908

facts.statement: Recent studies classify Cymbospondylus as the type genus of the family Cymbospondylidae, rather than Shastasauridae.
facts.quote: Cymbospondylus was formerly classified as a representative of the Shastasauridae, but more recent studies consider it to be more basal, view as the type genus of the Cymbospondylidae.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus is an extinct genus of large ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: Cymbospondylus (meaning "cupped vertebrae") is an extinct genus of large ichthyosaurs

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus possessed flippers for limbs and a fin on its tail.
facts.quote: As an ichthyosaur, Cymbospondylus had flippers for limbs and a fin on the tail.

facts.statement: The smallest species of Cymbospondylus reached a length of approximately 4 to 5 meters.
facts.quote: The different species of Cymbospondylus vary greatly in size, with the smallest reaching around 4 to 5 m in length.

facts.statement: The largest known species, C. youngorum, was estimated to be over 17 meters long, making it one of the largest animals of its time.
facts.quote: The largest known species, C. youngorum, is estimated over 17 m long, making Cymbospondylus one of the largest ichthyosaurs identified to date, but also one of the largest animals known of its time.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus lived in marine ecosystems alongside bivalves, ammonites, Saurichthys, coelacanths, hybodonts, sauropterygians, and other ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: Cymbospondylus lived in marine ecosystems alongside molluscs like bivalves and ammonites, bony fishes like Saurichthys and coelacanths, cartilaginous fishes like hybodonts, and marine reptiles like sauropterygians and other ichthyosaurs.

facts.statement: Joseph Leidy described Cymbospondylus in 1868 based on fossil vertebrae from Nevada, United States, which were transmitted to him by geologist Josiah Dwight Whitney.
facts.quote: In 1868, American paleontologist Joseph Leidy described two new genera of ichthyosaurs dating from the Middle Triassic on the basis of fossil vertebrae discovered in several localities in Nevada, United States, all of which were transmitted through the geologist Josiah Dwight Whitney.

facts.statement: The holotype of C. piscosus consists of five incomplete dorsal vertebrae discovered in the New Pass Range, northwest of Austin.
facts.quote: The holotype of C. piscosus is a block containing five incomplete dorsal vertebrae that was discovered in the New Pass Range, northwest of the city of Austin.

facts.statement: The name Cymbospondylus means "cupped vertebrae" in Ancient Greek, referring to the shape of the vertebrae.
facts.quote: The genus name Cymbospondylus derives from the Ancient Greek words κύμβη (kymbē, "cup") and σπόνδυλος (spondylos, "vertebra"), all taken together literally meaning cupped vertebrae, in reference to the rather obvious shape of this part of the skeleton.

facts.statement: Between 1901 and 1907, the University of California conducted ten expeditions across the United States to collect Triassic ichthyosaur fossils.
facts.quote: Between 1901 and 1907, the University of California sent ten expeditions across different corners of the United States to recover as many ichthyosaur fossils as possible dating from the Triassic, in order to be analyzed in more detail.

facts.statement: The University of California expeditions were led by Merriam and financed by Annie Montague Alexander.
facts.quote: These same expeditions were led by Merriam and were almost all financed by Annie Montague Alexander.

facts.statement: The expeditions collected more than fifty specimens of ichthyosaurs, each preserving significant portions of their skeletons.
facts.quote: The research finally collected more than fifty specimens, each preserving a significant portion of their skeletons.

facts.statement: In 2003, Christopher McGowan and Ryosuke Motani questioned the validity of C. piscosus, asserting its fossils lack distinctive characteristics.
facts.quote: In their work published in 2003, Christopher McGowan and Ryosuke Motani assert that the fossil vertebrae attributed to C. piscosus do not present distinctive characteristics to prove its validity.

facts.statement: McGowan and Motani suggested that the skeleton UCMP 9950 could be designated as a neotype for C. piscosus to resolve taxonomic issues.
facts.quote: To try to resolve this problem, the two authors suggest that the most complete known skeleton of C. petrinus (UCMP 9950) could be designated as a neotype of C. piscosus.

facts.statement: Established species of Cymbospondylus are known from Nevada and Switzerland, with unaffiliated specimens found in Idaho, the Alps, and Spitsbergen.
facts.quote: All established species of Cymbospondylus are known from the fossil records of Nevada and Switzerland, with referred specimens without specific affiliations having nevertheless been discovered in Idaho, the rest of the Alps and Spitsbergen, an island in Norway.

facts.statement: The European specimen PIMUZ T 4351 was formally described as C. buchseri by Paul Martin Sander in 1989, confirming the genus's presence in Europe.
facts.quote: The specimen in question, cataloged as PIMUZ T 4351, was formally described for the first time in 1989 under the name C. buchseri by Paul Martin Sander, thus confirming the presence of the genus in Europe.

facts.statement: Nadia Fröbisch and colleagues described the species C. nichollsi in 2006 based on an incomplete skeleton found in the Augusta Mountains.
facts.quote: In 2006, Nadia Fröbisch and colleagues described the species C. nichollsi based on an incomplete skeleton, cataloged as FMNH PR 2251, which was discovered in the Augusta Mountains.

facts.statement: The species C. nichollsi is named in honor of Elizabeth Nicholls, an American-Canadian paleontologist who specialized in Triassic marine reptiles.
facts.quote: The species in question is named in honor to Elizabeth Nicholls, an American-Canadian paleontologist specializing in Triassic marine reptiles, who made a major contribution to the ichthyosaurs that lived during this period.

facts.statement: A notable Cymbospondylus fossil was discovered in the Augusta Mountains in 2011 and exhumed in 2014.
facts.quote: In 2011, a notable new Cymbospondylus fossil was also discovered in the Augusta Mountains, then exhumed three years later in 2014.

facts.statement: The specimen LACM DI 158109 was formally designated the holotype for C. duelferi by Nicole Klein and colleagues in 2020.
facts.quote: However, it was only later that the specimen, cataloged as LACM DI 158109, was formally designated a holotype for the species C. duelferi by Nicole Klein and colleagues in 2020.

facts.statement: The species name C. duelferi honors Olaf Dülfer, a fossil preparer who contributed to research on Mesozoic marine reptiles.
facts.quote: The species name duelferi was chosen in honor of Olaf Dülfer, fossil preparer who made many practical contributions to research on Mesozoic marine reptiles.

facts.statement: Paul Sander discovered a notable Cymbospondylus specimen in the Augusta Mountains in 1998 and exhumed it with colleagues between 2014 and 2015.
facts.quote: In 1998, still in the Augusta Mountains, Sander discovered another notable specimen of Cymbospondylus, and exhumed it with his colleagues between 2014 and 2015.

facts.statement: A new species of Cymbospondylus was named in 2021 by Sander and colleagues based on a specimen discovered in the Augusta Mountains.
facts.quote: It was in 2021, one year after the identification of C. duelferi, that a new species of the genus was named from this specimen in Science by Sander and his colleagues.

facts.statement: The species C. youngorum is named in honor of Tom and Bonda Young, who financially supported the fossil exhumation project.
facts.quote: This species, C. youngorum, is named in honor of Tom and Bonda Young, these latter having financially supported the fossil exhumation project.

facts.statement: Three specimens from Idaho and Svalbard dated to the Olenekian stage of the Lower Triassic represent the oldest known members of the genus Cymbospondylus.
facts.quote: Three of these specimens, including one from Idaho, and two from the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard, are dated to the Olenekian stage of the Lower Triassic, making them the oldest known representatives of the genus.

facts.statement: A specimen from Monte Seceda, Italy, was initially referred to Shastasaurus sp. but was later attributed to Cymbospondylus in 1989, an attribution still recognized today.
facts.quote: The described specimen was first referred by the author to Shastasaurus sp., before being referred to Cymbospondylus in the official description of C. buchseri by Sander in 1989, an attribution which seems to still be recognized today.

facts.statement: Paul Sander described two specimens attributed to Cymbospondylus discovered in Spitsbergen, part of the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard, in 1992.
facts.quote: In 1992, Sander described two specimens attributed to Cymbospondylus having been discovered in different localities of Spitsbergen, located in the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard.

facts.statement: A well-preserved specimen consisting of 17 vertebrae and ribs was discovered in 1961 at Botneheia mountain in Svalbard and cataloged as PIMUZ A/III 496.
facts.quote: The first and the better preserved of the two specimens described in the article, consists of a series of 17 vertebrae associated with ribs which was discovered in 1961 in the Botneheia mountain, being cataloged as PIMUZ A/III 496.

facts.statement: Two isolated vertebrae cataloged as PIMUZ A/III 554 and 555 were discovered in the bay of Wichebukta in Svalbard.
facts.quote: The second consists of two isolated vertebrae, cataloged as PIMUZ A/III 554 and 555, which were both discovered in the bay of Wichebukta.

facts.statement: Judy A. Massare and Jack M. Callaway referred several fossils discovered in 1985 by H. Gregory McDonald in Idaho to Cymbospondylus in 1994.
facts.quote: In 1994, Judy A. Massare and Jack M. Callaway referred to a number of Cymbospondylus fossils discovered in 1985 by H. Gregory McDonald in the Platy Siltstone Member of the Thaynes Formation, in Idaho, United States.

facts.statement: In 2001, Olivier Rieppel and Fabio Marco Dalla Vecchia attributed two fossils from Forni di Sotto, Italy, with doubt to Cymbospondylus.
facts.quote: In 2001, Olivier Rieppel and Fabio Marco Dalla Vecchia listed a set of fossils of marine reptiles from the Triassic and having been discovered in the comune of Forni di Sotto, in Italy, including two that they attributed with doubt to Cymbospondylus.

facts.statement: The doubtful Cymbospondylus specimens from Forni di Sotto include one collection with a vertebra, neural spine, and rib fragments, and another with two isolated vertebrae.
facts.quote: The first of these collections consists of a single vertebra, a neural spine and three rib fragments, while the second consists of two isolated vertebrae.

facts.statement: Balini and Renesto described four partial vertebrae attributed to Cymbospondylus discovered in Piazza Brembana, Italy, in 2012.
facts.quote: In 2012, Balini and Renesto described four more or less partial vertebrae attributed to Cymbospondylus which were discovered in the comune of Piazza Brembana, in Italy, being cataloged MCSNB 11689 A, B, C, and D.

facts.statement: Numerous vertebrae attributed to Cymbospondylus were identified in the Vendomdalen Member of the Vikinghøgda Formation in Svalbard in 2013 and 2018.
facts.quote: In 2013 and 2018, numerous genus-assigned vertebrae were identified in the Vendomdalen Member of the Vikinghøgda Formation, Svalbard.

facts.statement: Leidy described the species Chonespondylus grandis in 1868 based on a caudal vertebra fragment from Star Canyon in the Humboldt Range.
facts.quote: In his 1868 paper describing Cymbospondylus, Leidy also named another ichthyosaur as Chonespondylus grandis, based on a fragment of a caudal vertebra found at Star Canyon in the Humboldt Range.

facts.statement: John Whitaker Hulke described the species Ichthyosaurus polaris in 1873 based on vertebrae and rib fragments found on Isfjorden, Spitsbergen, Norway.
facts.quote: In 1873, John Whitaker Hulke described a species of Ichthyosaurus, I. polaris, named after two sets of vertebrae associated with rib fragments that were discovered on Isfjorden, Spitsbergen, an island in Norway.

facts.statement: Merriam synonymized Chonespondylus grandis with Cymbospondylus petrinus in 1908 following the discovery of new complete fossils.
facts.quote: In 1908, after the discovery of new very complete fossils from C. petrinus, Merriam decided to definitively synonymize C. (?) grandis with the latter.

facts.statement: Carl Wiman transferred the species formerly known as Cymbospondylus polaris to the genus Pessosaurus in 1910.
facts.quote: In 1910, the species was moved to the newly erected genus Pessosaurus by Carl Wiman, as P. polaris, to which it has always been referred by this name ever since.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene described two Cymbospondylus species in 1916 from fossils found in the Muschelkalk of Laufenburg, Baden-Württemberg.
facts.quote: In a review of German ichthyosaurs published in 1916, Friedrich von Huene described two other species of Cymbospondylus whose fossils were discovered in the Muschelkalk of the town of Laufenburg in the state of Baden-Württemberg.

facts.statement: Chun Li and Hai-Lu You named Cymbospondylus asiaticus in 2002 based on a complete skull from the Xiaowa Formation in Guizhou Province, China.
facts.quote: In 2002, paleontologists Chun Li and Hai-Lu You named a new species as C. asiaticus based on a complete skull discovered in the Xiaowa Formation, located in Guizhou Province, China, and it was considered as the most recent known representative of the genus.

facts.statement: Authors expressed doubt in 2006 about attributing the species C. nichollsi to the genus Cymbospondylus.
facts.quote: In the official description of C. nichollsi published in 2006, the authors are doubtful regarding the attribution of this species to Cymbospondylus.

facts.statement: While the color of Cymbospondylus is unknown, some early ichthyosaurs likely had uniformly dark skin, evidenced by preserved eumelanin pigments.
facts.quote: Although the colour of Cymbospondylus is unknown, at least some ichthyosaurs may have been uniformly dark-coloured in life, which is evidenced by the discovery of high concentrations of eumelanin pigments in the preserved skin of an early ichthyosaur fossil.

facts.statement: The classification of Guizhouichthyosaurus tangae as a synonym of Shastasaurus was contested in 2010, with Michael W. Maisch provisionally reclassifying it as a distinct genus.
facts.quote: However, considering that Guizhouichthyosaurus is similar to Shastasaurus, they moved the species as S. tangae. This synonymy was contested the following year, in 2010, in which Michael W. Maisch provisionally reclassified Guizhouichthyosaurus as a distinct genus.

facts.statement: Recent phylogenetic and morphological analyses consider Guizhouichthyosaurus to be a distinct genus from Shastasaurus.
facts.quote: However, numerous phylogenetic and morphological analyzes subsequently published consider Guizhouichthyosaurus to be distinct genus from Shastasaurus.

facts.statement: C. youngorum is estimated to reach 17.65 meters in length and weigh 44.7 metric tons, making it one of the largest ichthyosaurs known.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of C. youngorum having a skull measuring almost 2 m long and its humerus being the second largest bone of this type recorded in an ichthyosaur, the maximum size of the animal is therefore estimated at 17.65 m for a weight of 44.7 MT.

facts.statement: Researchers describe C. youngorum as "the first aquatic giant" due to its early Middle Triassic age and massive size.
facts.quote: The antiquity as well as such an imposing size for an animal dating from the beginning of the Middle Triassic makes C. youngorum qualify as "the first aquatic giant" according to Lene Liebe Delsett and Nicholas David Pyenson.

facts.statement: The size of C. nichollsi is difficult to estimate because its holotype fossil preserves only half of the skull.
facts.quote: Estimating the size of C. nichollsi is more complex, because although the holotype specimen is known from a significant portion of the skeleton, the latter preserves only half of the skull.

facts.statement: Some Cymbospondylus specimens with undetermined species attribution are known only from thin fossil remains.
facts.quote: Individuals with undetermined specific attributions have also been given estimates regarding their size, although known from thinner fossil remains.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus has an elongated, conical snout where the premaxillae and nasal bones are the largest skull elements.
facts.quote: Like other ichthyosaurs, the snout of Cymbospondylus is elongated into a long, conical rostrum, the largest bones of which are the premaxillae and nasal bones.

facts.statement: The shape of the superior temporal fenestra varies by species, being oval in C. nichollsi and C. duelferi but triangular in C. petrinus.
facts.quote: The shape of the superior temporal fenestra differs between some species, being oval in C. nichollsi and C. duelferi but triangular in C. petrinus.

facts.statement: The number of scleral ring ossicles varies among species, ranging from 12 in C. duelferi to 14-18 in C. petrinus.
facts.quote: The number of bony elements constituting the scleral rings varies between species: 12 ossicles in C. duelferi; 13 ossicles in C. buchseri; 14 ossicles in C. nichollsi; and between 14 and 18 ossicles in C. petrinus.

facts.statement: The sagittal crest is low in C. duelferi and C. nichollsi, high in C. petrinus, and completely absent in C. youngorum.
facts.quote: The sagittal crest is more or less pronounced in the different species, being low in C. duelferi and C. nichollsi, clearly high in C. petrinus, and totally absent in C. youngorum.

facts.statement: C. petrinus exhibits a unique form of thecodont dentition where teeth appear fused at the base of the sockets.
facts.quote: C. petrinus has a particular form of thecodont dentition, its teeth appearing to be fused at the bottom of the alveoli.

facts.statement: C. duelferi has subthecodont dentition, characterized by teeth implanted in shallow sockets.
facts.quote: C. duelferi has a subthecodont type of dentition, meaning that its teeth are implanted in shallow sockets.

facts.statement: C. youngorum possesses a thick bone base attaching to the teeth, a trait not observed in other ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: C. youngorum has a thick base of the bone attaching to the teeth, a trait not seen in other ichthyosaurs.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus teeth are homodont, sharing an identical conical, ridged, and pointed shape.
facts.quote: The teeth are homodont, that is to say they share an identical shape, being conical, ridged and pointed.

facts.statement: Tooth counts are known for three species: C. duelferi has over 21 upper teeth, C. petrinus has 30-35 teeth per jaw, and C. youngorum has 43 upper and over 31 lower teeth.
facts.quote: Only three species were able to have a more or less clear estimate of their number of teeth: C. duelferi having a number greater than 21 teeth known in the upper jaw, but unknown in the lower jaw; C. petrinus with between 30 and 35 teeth in the upper and lower jaws; and C. youngorum having 43 teeth in the upper jaw and more than 31 teeth in the lower jaw.

facts.statement: It is agreed that Cymbospondylus is a basal member of the Ichthyosauria clade.
facts.quote: However it is agreed upon that Cymbospondylus is a rather basal member of the clade.

facts.statement: A 2021 analysis places Cymbospondylus at the base of Ichthyosauria, outside the derived Hueneosauria group.
facts.quote: In the analysis of Bindellini et al. (2021), Cymbospondylus is placed at the very base of Ichthyosauria, outside the more derived members of Hueneosauria (including Mixosauridae and Shastasauridae).

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis recovers C. youngorum as the most derived member of a Nevada clade, with C. buchseri at the base.
facts.quote: The description of C. youngorum further supports this Nevadan clade, recovering C. youngorum as its most derived member while C. buchseri from Europe sits at the base of the genus.

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus has a convoluted taxonomy, with some researchers suggesting the type species should be neglected.
facts.quote: This causes Cymbospondylus to have a very convoluted taxonomy, with it being suggested that the type species should be neglected.

facts.statement: Researchers could not determine a definite placement for C. buchseri and stated further study is needed to confirm if it belongs to the genus.
facts.quote: In their phylogenetic analysis the authors did not recover a definite placement for C. buchseri, leading them to state that further study was needed to determine whether the Swiss species belonged to the genus.

facts.statement: C. youngorum lived at the beginning of the Middle Triassic.
facts.quote: The antiquity as well as such an imposing size for an animal dating from the beginning of the Middle Triassic makes C. youngorum qualify as "the first aquatic giant" according to Lene Liebe Delsett and Nicholas David Pyenson.

facts.statement: The largest known species, C. youngorum, had a skull measuring up to about 2 meters long.
facts.quote: the largest known species of Cymbospondylus, C. youngorum, has a skull up to about 2 m long

facts.statement: Direct fossil evidence shows that C. buchseri ate soft-bodied coleoid cephalopods, as its stomach contents contained only their hooks.
facts.quote: Direct evidence for its diet exists for the medium-sized Cymbospondylus buchseri from Switzerland, which was found with its stomach contents exclusively consisting of hooks belonging to soft-bodied coleoid cephalopods

facts.statement: Researchers suggest C. buchseri had a robust rostrum that supported a forceful feeding strategy with high bite force.
facts.quote: Bindellini and colleagues suggest that C. buchseri may have employed a more forceful feeding strategy with a slower feeding cycle and a higher biteforce, supported by the animal's robust rostrum

facts.statement: C. youngorum is inferred to have been a generalist predator of squid and fish, based on its blunt conical teeth and elongated rostrum.
facts.quote: For C. youngorum a generalist diet of squid and fish is inferred based on the blunt and conical teeth in combination with the elongated rostrum

facts.statement: It is debated whether C. youngorum also fed on large-bodied vertebrates, including other Cymbospondylus species.
facts.quote: However, as with C. buchseri, Sander et al. entertain the possibility that C. youngorum could have fed on large-bodied vertebrates as well, including the other Cymbospondylus species of the region

facts.statement: The holotype of C. duelferi contains three strings of small vertebrae interpreted as the remains of three fetuses.
facts.quote: The holotype of C. duelferi preserves three small strings of articulated vertebrae located within the trunk region of the specimen

facts.statement: Fossil evidence suggests Cymbospondylus gave live birth to at least three offspring.
facts.quote: Following this interpretation, Cymbospondylus would have given live birth to a minimum of three offspring

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus lived alongside other abundant ichthyosaurs like Omphalosaurus, Phalarodon, and the large Thalattoarchon in the Fossil Hill Member.
facts.quote: The most abundant marine reptiles of the Fossil Hill Member are the ichthyosaurs, including Cymbospondylus itself, Omphalosaurus, Phalarodon and the large Thalattoarchon

facts.statement: The fossil assemblage indicates that the ancient surface waters where Cymbospondylus lived were well aerated.
facts.quote: The significant presence of marine reptiles, ammonites and other invertebrates in the Fossil Hill Member indicates that the surface waters were well aerated

facts.statement: The only known specimen of C. buschseri comes from the Besano Formation in Switzerland.
facts.quote: The only currently known specimen of C. buschseri is recorded from the Besano Formation, also known as the Grenzbitumenzone in Switzerland.

facts.statement: Fossils date from the end of the Anisian to the beginning of the Ladinian stages.
facts.quote: This formation is located in the Alps and extends from southern Switzerland to northern Italy, containing numerous fossils dating from between the end of the Anisian and the beginning of the Ladinian.

facts.statement: The animal lived in a marine lagoon on the western side of the Tethys Ocean.
facts.quote: During the time when the animal lived, when the Besano Formation was being deposited, the region where Monte San Giorgio is would have been a marine lagoon, located in a basin on the western side of the Tethys Ocean.

facts.statement: Researchers estimate the lagoon was between 30 and 130 meters deep.
facts.quote: Researchers estimate that this same lagoon would have reached between 30 – 130 m deep.

facts.statement: Near-surface waters were well oxygenated and inhabited by plankton and free-swimming organisms.
facts.quote: The near-surface waters would have been well oxygenated and were inhabited by a wide range of plankton and free-swimming organisms.

facts.statement: Poor water circulation resulted in anoxic, oxygen-deprived water at the bottom of the lagoon.
facts.quote: However, water circulation within the lagoon was poor, resulting in typically anoxic water at the bottom, deprived of oxygen.

facts.statement: The presence of terrestrial fossils like conifers and land reptiles indicates the region was near land.
facts.quote: The presence of terrestrial fossils, such as conifers and land-dwelling reptiles indicates that the region would have been near land.

facts.statement: Thalattoarchon was likely the only contemporary apex predator, probably attacking smaller marine reptiles or juveniles.
facts.quote: Due to its large and sharp teeth, Thalattoarchon would probably have been the only apex predator with which Cymbospondylus was contemporary, probably attacking smaller marine reptiles, or even juveniles.

facts.statement: Stomach contents of Mixosaurus cornalianus show remains of small coleoids and fish, suggesting it hunted smaller prey than larger relatives.
facts.quote: The stomach contents of Mixosaurus cornalianus show the remains of small coleoids and fish, suggesting that it would have gone after smaller prey than its larger relatives.

facts.statement: The genus was described by Leidy in 1868.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Leidy, 1868

facts.statement: Known species include C. buchseri, C. petrinus, C. piscosus, and C. nichollsi.
facts.quote: subdivision: C. buchseri Liu & Sander, 1989 C. petrinus Leidy, 1868 C. piscosus Leidy, 1868 (especie tipo) C. nichollsi Fröbisch, Sander & Rieppel, 2006

facts.statement: Cymbospondylus lived in what is now North America and Europe during the middle Triassic period.
facts.quote: Cymbospondylus es un ictiosaurio que vivió en lo que hoy es Norteamérica y Europa a mediados del período Triásico.

facts.statement: This marine reptile had two pairs of flippers and an eel-like tail, lacking a dorsal fin, with a length of approximately 6 to 10 meters.
facts.quote: Este reptil marino tenía 2 pares de aletas y una cola parecida a la de las anguilas y debido a ser uno de los primeros reptiles marinos ictiosauros, era el ictiosaurio menos parecido a los peces ya que este no poseía la aleta dorsal; con una longitud aproximada de 6 a 10 metros.

facts.statement: Its skull was curved and had sharp teeth for eating reptiles, primitive amphibians, and cephalopods such as Ammonites.
facts.quote: Su cráneo era curvado y tenía dientes afilados para comer reptiles, anfibios primitivos y cefalópodos tales como el Ammonites.

facts.statement: Fossils have been found in Nevada, USA, and Switzerland.
facts.quote: Sus fósiles han sido hallados en Nevada (EE. UU.) y Suiza de este espécimen descienden la mayoría de los ictiosauros más estilizados del Cretácico.

facts.statement: The Cymbospondylus appeared in the 2003 BBC docufiction Sea Monsters.
facts.quote: Sea Monsters fue emitida en el 2003, producida por la BBC y emitida por primera vez en la televisión británica.

facts.statement: In the show, it is depicted as an alpha predator of its time and one of the earliest species of the order Ichthyosauria.
facts.quote: En el, se muestra al Cymbospondylus como depredador alfa de su época y una de las primeras especies del orden Ichthyosauria.

facts.statement: There are 17 recorded fossil occurrences for the genus.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 17

rejected.quote: The animal has a skull with a long, thin snout, proportionally small eye sockets, an elongated trunk, and a less pronounced tail than in later ichthyosaurs.

rejected.statement: Cymbospondylus had conical, pointed teeth with longitudinal ridges, indicating a diet of fish, cephalopods, and possibly other marine reptiles for larger species.
rejected.quote: The teeth are conical and pointed, having longitudinal ridges, indicating a diet of fishes and cephalopods, and possibly other marine reptiles for larger species.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'cephalopods and possibly other marine reptiles for larger'

rejected.statement: John Campbell Merriam assigned C. piscosus as the type species of Cymbospondylus in 1902, as no type species was designated in the original 1868 description.
rejected.quote: As no type species was designated in the 1868 article, it was not until 1902 that John Campbell Merriam assigned C. piscosus to this title
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'as no type species was designated in the'

rejected.statement: A partial skeleton of a large ichthyosaur was discovered in 1927 at the Monte San Giorgio fossil site in Switzerland and first mentioned by Bernhard Peyer in 1944.
rejected.quote: In 1927, a partial skeleton of a large ichthyosaur was discovered in the Grenzbitumenzone Member at the Monte San Giorgio fossil site in Switzerland and was mentioned by Bernhard Peyer in 1944.
